target_customer: Employers and recruiters buying prepaid click based job ads aimed at developers; publishers were programming blogs that earned a revenue share
problem: Recruiters had to reach passive developer candidates where they spent time online; Snaptalent served job ads across publisher sites and targeted visitors by employer or university inferred from IP address.
business_model: Pay per click ad network, advertisers prepaid 250 dollars per 500 clicks, publishers got an undisclosed revenue share

founders.name: Sumon Sadhu
education: Left a PhD to help start Snaptalent (field and school not stated)
founders.background_notes: YC page lists him as founder and CEO. Startups.co.uk profile says Paul Graham recruited him to set up the US company. Dealroom lists three other founders (Jamie Quint, Tim Davey, Brad Cater) but no company source confirms them, so they are not listed here.

exit.reason: Company message said the model was economically unviable; it also cited the 2009 recession and returned most of the capital to investors.

competitors.name: Edgeio
competitors.what: Classifieds and job listing aggregator the launch article called the closest earlier offering
competitors.traction_then: Had already shut down by March 2008, per TechCrunch

competitors.name: Indeed, SimplyHired and ZamZim
competitors.what: Job aggregators that the launch article grouped as the existing online job site category

competitors.name: Monster, HotJobs and Jobster
competitors.what: Destination job sites that employers already paid for listings

technical_complexity.rationale: An ad serving network with a publisher widget and IP to employer or university matching needs ad delivery, geo and organization lookup and billing, which is more than CRUD for a two person team.

defensibility.rationale: The IP targeting idea was copyable and a two sided network needed supply from publishers; only 16 programming blogs had signed at launch.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent copied or bought it; the company itself shut down in August 2009.

market_need_then: Developer hiring was competitive in 2008 and recruiters wanted to reach passive candidates, but the launch article said no direct competitor existed and the company later called its own model economically unviable.

identity.voice_and_tone: The shutdown message was addressed to investors, users and fans and was candid about the economics

branding.community_and_virality: Covered by TechCrunch at launch in March 2008 and on the YC blog at shutdown; the startups.co.uk profile called it controversial for its IP targeting. No merch or fan community found.

brand_strength.rationale: Little brand evidence beyond launch coverage and a shutdown post; the product was an ad network so the brand mattered less than publisher supply.

pivots.why: ERE reported the company moved from the ad network to a college recruiting idea within months before closing; date not exact and only seen in one outlet snippet

outcome_analysis: Snaptalent launched in March 2008 with a two sided ad network for developer job ads and 16 publisher blogs. It never found a viable economic model, and in August 2009 it announced it was shutting down and returning most of the capital to investors, citing unviable economics and the recession. The YC blog post and ERE coverage give the cause in the company's own words, and a reported late attempt to pivot toward college recruiting did not save it.
notes: Snaptalent has no company website listed on YC. The 125,000 dollar seed rests on a single database (Dealroom) and Seedtable shows a date but no amount. The 1.5 million dollar backing figure comes from one outlet (Startups.co.uk, which says it launched in March with 1.5 million dollars of backing) and is not stated as a round, so its stage is other; the two figures may overlap. The pivot detail comes from a search summary of an ERE article that was not opened. Other listings place the company in London; YC lists London and San Francisco.
